title: Aquinas, again
tomorrow: what's the very first word of Benedict's Rule?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Catechism's four pillars: believe, celebrate, live, pray. Today, the man whose thinking runs under a lot of that book.

A pickup game after school. A freshman misses an easy pass, and the yelling is out before you can stop it. Afterward, the quiet thought: maybe holy people just aren't built like me. Maybe being good means turning the competitive part off. Thomas Aquinas, the Dominican friar who wrote the Summa, gives a different answer, and it's one line long: grace does not destroy nature, it perfects it.
screen: `THE YELLING GETS OUT FIRST.` → `TURN THE DRIVE OFF?` → `AQUINAS: A DIFFERENT ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Start where Aquinas starts: what you are is good. Genesis says, in the Douay-Rheims Bible, "God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good." Sin wounds that goodness, but it doesn't turn it into something else. So when grace comes, God's own life given freely, it doesn't swap you out for a calmer person. It heals what's wounded and finishes what's there, the way a coach doesn't hand you someone else's legs but trains the ones you have. A sharp mind becomes a mind that seeks truth. A big heart becomes a heart that loves well. And a competitive streak? Paul didn't ask athletes to stop. He wrote to the Corinthians: "So run that you may obtain." Here's the one to tell a friend: Aquinas says not all anger is sin. In the Summa he argues that anger ruled by reason, aimed at what's truly wrong, can even be good; anger that runs ahead of reason is the problem. So grace doesn't delete the fire. It teaches the fire where to burn. That doesn't excuse the yelling. The pass was missed, not a wrong done, and the anger ran ahead of reason. Grace works there too: an apology, a cooler head next time, a drive that lifts the freshman instead of flattening her. The same nature, perfected, not erased.
screen: `WHAT YOU ARE IS GOOD.` · `GRACE HEALS AND FINISHES.` · `SO RUN THAT YOU MAY OBTAIN.` · `ANGER RULED BY REASON.` · then, large: `GRACE PERFECTS.`

segments.voice: Count three things about how you're made: a strength, a quirk, and something people have called too much. For each one, if you pray, you can say a quiet thank you to God for it; if not, name each one as good, the way Genesis does, and let it stay.
Aquinas. Thomas Aquinas, friar and teacher, who saw grace finishing nature instead of fighting it.
Your line: grace perfects, finishing what God already called very good, competitive streak included. See you tomorrow.
